fetched_contents.text: Influence factors associated with fertility intention among people living with HIV in China and other regions: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Advances in medical care and improved quality of life have fostered a growing desire for parenthood among people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, this desire remains inadequately addressed in China, highlighting a crucial research gap. Understanding the factors influencing fertility intentions in PLHIV is essential for informing policy development. Methods We conducted a systematic review of English and Chinese literature, analyzing articles from 2000 to 2024. The odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was used for pooled measurement. Subgroup analyses based on regional factors were performed, and publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test. Results The review included 25 articles with 11,394 participants. Key factors associated with fertility intention included age (OR = 2.67, 95%CI: 2.04–3.48, P < 0.05), marital status (OR = 1.52, 95%CI: 1.14–2.02, P < 0.05), and number of children (OR = 5.28, 95%CI: 3.58–7.79, P < 0.05). Interestingly, education level did not significantly impact fertility desire (OR = 1.08, 95%CI: 0.72–1.41, P = 0.61). Subgroup analysis revealed that childlessness was a stronger influence in China (OR = 7.40, 95%CI: 3.76–14.58, P < 0.05) compared to developing and developed countries, where higher education levels had minimal or even negative effects on fertility intentions (OR = 0.98, 95%CI: 0.66–1.46, P = 0.93). No significant differences were observed regarding age and marital status between China and other regions. Conclusions This study highlights the prominent roles of age, marital status, and number of children in shaping fertility intentions among PLHIV. In China, the social and national context uniquely influences these intentions. Given the limited number of studies and variability in educational classifications across countries, further in-depth research is warranted. Keywords: Fertility intention, HIV, People living with HIV, Influence factors Background Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) poses a significant threat to human health by weakening the immune system, and it continues to challenge global public health efforts through its impact on vulnerable populations [1]. As of the end of 2023, the Joint United Nations Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) reported approximately 39.9 million individuals living with HIV worldwide [2]. Notably, it is documented that nearly 90% of new child HIV infections worldwide result from mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) [3]. Concerns regarding the health implications for future generations and other health-related factors have historically led many individuals diagnosed with HIV to forgo parenthood or express the diminished desire for children [4]. However, advancements in medical care and improvements in quality of life have mitigated some of these concerns, leading to a notable resurgence in the desire to marry and have children among this demographic [5–9]. Sociodemographic factors have emerged as primary factors impacting the fertility intention of PLHIV. Studies have shown that factors such as age, gender, family income, occupation type, education level, marital status, number of children, sexual partners, and religion play vital roles in shaping these desires [10]. The utilization of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) has exhibited a significant association with heightened fertility intention among PLHIV [11]. Panozzo’s findings suggest an increased inclination toward having children due to improved health on ART [11, 12]. Notably, while ART has enhanced fertility desires, it has not necessarily led to a proportional rise in actual fertility rates [13]. Moreover, studies, including one from South Africa, highlight a complex relationship between ART usage and parenthood aspirations [4]. Research by Demissie (2014) and Mekonnen (2017) corroborate similar findings regarding the impact of age and marital status on fertility desires within the HIV patient demographic. They postulate that younger HIV patients exhibit a stronger desire for parenthood compared to their older counterparts, and most unmarried individuals also point to this result because they may be eager to have children due to aspirations for an ideal family size [14, 15]. Despite extensive studies focusing on diverse populations globally, a comprehensive comparative analysis of PLHIV’s fertility intentions, particularly in China, is lacking. As the largest developing nation with a rich cultural heritage, China has experienced significant international exchanges since its reform policies. Although its HIV prevalence is relatively low at 0.09% compared to the UK (0.15%) and the US (0.34%), the sheer size of its population results in a considerable number of infected individuals [16]. This context necessitates an exploration of the factors influencing the desire for parenthood among PLHIV in China compared to other regions. This study aims to delineate the factors influencing fertility intentions among PLHIV in China and to compare these findings with other geographical locations. By addressing this knowledge gap, the research will provide practical fertility-related guidance for PLHIV both domestically and internationally. fetched_contents.text: Meta-analyses of fertility desires of people living with HIV Abstract Background Literature review has shown that some years back the fertility desires of people living with HIV was low but in the recent years, it was reported as increasing. However, little is known about the strength of association of fertility desire of HIV positive people with antiretroviral therapy (ART) experience, age, sex, education level, and number of children. Methods In these meta-analyses, twenty studies from different parts of the world were included. The odds ratios of fertility desires were determined using the random-effects model. Heterogeneity among the studies was assessed by computing values for Tau2, Chi-square (Q), I2 and P-value. Sensitivity analysis and funnel plot were done to assess the stability of pooled values to outliers and publication bias, respectively. Results The pooled analysis demonstrated that fertility desires of study participants had no association with ART. Similarly, the overall odds ratio did not show statistically significant association of fertility desires with sex and educational attainment of study participants although forest plots of some studies fall on increased and some others on decreased sides of fertility desires. The two variables that demonstrated a strong association with fertility desires were age less than 30 years and being childless. The lowest heterogeneity was found in a meta-analysis comparing ART experienced and ART naïve HIV positive people. In all meta-analyses, the sensitivity analyses showed the stability of the pooled odds ratios; and the funnel plots did not show publication or disclosure bias. Conclusion Although the fertility desires among childless and younger age group was very strong, we realized that quite a significant segment of HIV-infected people have desire for fertility. Therefore, including fertility issue as integral part of HIV patient care may help several of them in their reproductive decision making (letting them know the risks and methods of prevention while anticipating pregnancy). Keywords: ART, Fertility desire, Meta-analysis, HIV positive, Sensitivity analysis Background Before the era of HIV, wishing to have a biological child and preserving the continuity of their family to the future generation is perhaps a common thought of all and this is also expected to be same in these days in the majority of individuals who are sero-negative for HIV. However, several studies have shown that the fertility desire of people living with HIV was found to be significantly reduced [1-4]. A national survey in Cameroon revealed that women’s fertility desire was about 55% and the main factor independently associated with this desire was having good physical health [5]. In other African countries, the fertility desires were 15% in Malawi [6], 18% in Uganda [7], 41% in Ethiopia [4] and 63% in Nigeria [8]. One of US studies also showed that the majority of HIV positive women did not have desires to be pregnant [9]. On the other hand, the fertility desire of HIV-infected individuals were reported as increasing because of increasing hope of living longer with ART, resumption of a healthy life, and the overall physical and mental well-being. A multivariate analysis from Uganda showed that the fertility desire of HIV-infected individuals had significantly increased with ART [10]. In Canada, the proportion of fertility desire among HIV positive women increased from about 26% in 2007 [11] to 69% in 2009 [12]. Since majorities of HIV positive women are in the reproductive age, a decade back the fertility desire was also predicted that many will continue to have desire for children [13]. This is because; parenthood, particularly among married couples, is an important component of their social status. As noted by two qualitative studies (South Africa and Zimbabwe), the availability of ART and prevention of perinatal HIV transmission has also positively affected childbearing desires [14,15]. Several non-comparative studies have also shown the independent association of other factors with fertility desire in HIV-infected population. A partner’s desire for a child was one of the strongest predictors for women’s fertility desire [16]. In another study, being younger age, having fewer living children and higher quality of life were individually associated with fertility desire [17]. In general, a systematic review including twenty nine studies has also outlined the presence of many more factors that are related to fertility desires [18]. However, by design, it was not a quantitative or pooled analysis to more powerfully estimate the true effect size. Furthermore, from previously published primary studies, it was noted that the association of fertility desire with ART, age, sex, education level, and number of children were inconsistent. Thus, the objective of this pooled analysis was to demonstrate the strength of association of these variables with fertility desire. fetched_contents.text: Prevalence and factors associated with fertility desire among people living with HIV: A systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background The fertility desire of people living with HIV (PLHIV) has been rising in the past decade. However, there are many studies among which the association remains controversial between the fertility desire of HIV-infected persons and antiretroviral therapy (ART), sex, marital status, and educational level. Methods We performed a literature search of these meta-analyses in PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science and ScienceDirect in November 2019. We also reviewed references of eligible studies to complement the search. We used pooled odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) with a random-effects model and a fixed-effects model to estimate the association between fertility desire among PLHIV and ART, sex, age, marital status, educational level, and number of children. Subgroups with I square values (I2) and sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the heterogeneity and the stability of the overall ORs, respectively. We evaluated publication bias using Egger’s test and a visual inspection of the symmetry in funnel plots. Results In these meta-analyses 50 articles were included with 22,367 subjects. The pooled prevalence of fertility desire among PLHIV was estimated to be 42.04%. The pooled analyses showed that the fertility desire of PLHIV is associated with ART (OR = 1.11, 95% CI:1.00–1.23, P = 0.043), sex (OR = 1.51, 95% CI:1.10–2.09), age (OR = 2.65, 95% CI:2.24–3.14), marital status (OR = 1.34, 95% CI:1.08–1.66), educational level (OR = 0.85, 95% CI:0.73–1.00, P = 0.047) and the number of children (OR = 3.99, 95% CI:3.06–5.20). PLHIV who are on ART, are male, are younger than 30, are married/cohabiting, have received a secondary education or above, and are childless have a higher prevalence of fertility desire. The two factors of age and the number of children, in particular demonstrated a strong significant association with fertility desire. We found moderate heterogeneity in the meta-analyses of age and educational level and high heterogeneity in the meta-analyses of sex, marital status and number of children. Publication bias was detected in the meta-analyses of the association of fertility with sex and educational level. Conclusion This study demonstrates that the prevalence of fertility desire among HIV-infected people is 42.04%, and the fertility desire among PLHIV is associated with ART experience, sex, age, marital status, the number of children, and educational level. Since a majority of PLHIV are of reproductive age, it is necessary to support PLHIV in terms of their needs regarding reproductive decision-making. Through counseling and reproductive health care, further measures to prevent the horizontal and vertical transmission of HIV should be taken. Introduction According to the 2019 reports of Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), there were approximately 37.9 million people living with HIV (PLHIV) across the world, among whom 1.47 million were of reproductive age [1]. It is common for them to want to get married and start a family. However, the prevalence of fertility desire/intention among PLHIV has been low for the past two decades due to poor health status, fear of infecting one’s spouse or fetus, and discouraging policies in many countries [2]. In 2000, a study conducted in Europe showed that the pregnancy rate trended to decrease in women after receiving a diagnosis of HIV while the rate of abortion had increased [3]. Lewis et al showed that HIV-infected women in Sub-Saharan Africa have a lower fertility rate than their non-infected counterparts [4]. With more access to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), nevertheless, the quality of life for PLHIV has significantly improved, and their life span is expected to be longer [5, 6]. As a result, their fertility desire or intention has risen [7, 8]. A study from Ethiopia indicated that the prevalence of fertility desire among HIV-positive individuals increased from 20.0% in 2010 to 42.1% in 2013 [9, 10]. A similar growing tendency toward the desire to reproduce has been found in other regions as well [11]. A number of studies have pointed to many factors that could influence the fertility desire of PLHIV. For example, HIV-positive individuals who are young tend to have a higher prevalence of fertility desire [12, 13]. Decreased fertility desire is related to divorce or separation compared to being married, and to having at least one child in contrast to having no children [12–14]. Several studies have revealed that educational status is a predicator of fertility desire [15]. In addition, HIV disclosure to sexual partners could affect the fertility desire of HIV-infected people [14, 16]. Since the fertility desires of PLHIV is tied to sexual practices and pregnancy, it is crucial to prevent horizontal transmission between partners and mother-to-child transmission (MTCT). Previous studies indicate that the viral load of PLHIV on ART could be suppressed; therefore, the risk of transmitting HIV to sexual partners could decrease or even be eliminated [17]. Many measures for sero-discordant couples, such as artificial insemination, timed unprotected intercourse, assisted reproductive techniques, sperm washing and pre-exposure prophylaxis, could be used to reduce HIV horizontal transmission [18–20]. There are also many means of preventing the mother-to-child transmission of HIV (PMTCT), including HIV testing and counseling, the use of ARV drugs, safe delivery, and safe breastfeeding. As a consequence, fertility desire among PLHIV not only has significant implications for such individuals, their partners, and fetuses, but also plays a critical role in preventing HIV transmission and providing reproductive health care. Direct evidence for higher fertility intentions among married HIV-positive individuals comes from a few studies and reviews, but the strongest support is not uniform across all settings and measurements.

The most directly relevant evidence is the meta-analysis on fertility intention among people living with HIV (PLHIV), which found that marital status was associated with fertility intention. In the 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 25 articles with 11,394 participants, marital status was linked to higher fertility intention with an odds ratio of 1.52 (95% CI: 1.14–2.02) [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis in the same field found that married/cohabiting PLHIV had higher fertility desire than single, widowed, or divorced individuals, with similar wording and directionality in the evidence [N6-F3]. A separate systematic review and meta-analysis also reported that marital status was associated with fertility desire, with an odds ratio of 1.34 (95% CI: 1.08–1.66) [N3-F3]. These studies together indicate a consistent pattern: married or cohabiting PLHIV are more likely to have higher fertility intention/desire than unmarried peers.

On measurement, the evidence is somewhat mixed. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis used odds ratios for pooled measurement of fertility intention, but it does not give a detailed account of the exact instruments used in each study [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on fertility desire among PLHIV also reported pooled odds ratios and used random-effects models, with subgroup analyses and sensitivity assessments, but again it does not specify the exact measurement tool in every study [N1-F2]. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis explicitly states that the association was analyzed using pooled odds ratios and random-effects models, and it reports marital status as a significant factor [N3-F3]. So while the measurement is not always identical across studies, the core construct is generally treated as a binary or categorical indicator of fertility desire/ intention, and the evidence base is reasonably consistent in direction.

The findings are not limited to a single region or treatment status, but they do show regional variation and treatment-related caveats. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis notes that no significant differences were observed between China and other regions for age and marital status, but it also emphasizes that the study design and educational classifications varied across countries [N1-F1]. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis includes 50 articles with 22,367 subjects and reports that fertility desire was associated with ART, sex, age, marital status, educational level, and number of children [N3-F3]. This suggests the findings extend beyond a single treatment status, but they are still best interpreted as generally positive for married individuals rather than as universal across all HIV-positive populations.

In short, the direct evidence supports higher fertility intentions among married HIV-positive people in several studies and meta-analyses [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-F3]. However, the evidence is strongest when marital status is treated as a categorical indicator, and it is not always fully consistent in measurement detail or universally generalizable across regions and treatment statuses [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence base for marital-status differences in fertility intentions is useful but has important limitations.

Study design strengths include broad coverage and quantitative synthesis. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 25 articles with 11,394 participants is large and includes pooled odds ratios, subgroup analyses, and assessment of publication bias [N1-F1]. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 50 articles with 22,367 subjects similarly uses pooled odds ratios, random-effects models, and sensitivity analyses, and it evaluates heterogeneity and publication bias [N3-F3]. These designs are strong for identifying consistent associations, especially when the effect is large and the sample size is sufficient. However, the evidence is still mainly observational and cross-sectional, so causal inference is limited [N1-F1][N3-F3].

A major limitation is setting and follow-up. The 2024 systematic review notes that the included literature spans 2000–2024 and is from China and other regions, but it also highlights variability in educational classifications across countries and limited studies in some settings [N1-F1]. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis includes articles from many parts of the world but reports moderate to high heterogeneity for some factors, including marital status [N3-F3]. This heterogeneity suggests that the association may not be uniform across contexts. The evidence also does not consistently report follow-up or longitudinal data on fertility intentions, so it is unclear how stable the association is over time [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Confounding factors are likely to explain some of the apparent differences. The 2024 review explicitly lists age, marital status, and number of children as prominent factors shaping fertility intentions, and it notes that childlessness was especially strong in China [N1-F1]. The 2021 meta-analysis similarly identifies age, marital status, educational level, number of children, and ART as associated factors [N3-F3]. This implies that marital status may be linked to other variables that influence fertility intentions, such as age, number of children, and social context. The evidence also mentions that HIV-related stigma and disclosure may vary by marital status, which is relevant because stigma can influence reproductive decisions [N2-R3]. In addition, fertility desire is tied to sociodemographic and psychosocial factors, including family lineage pressure and economic utility [N4-R1][N4-R3]. These confounders make it difficult to isolate marital status as the sole driver of higher fertility intention.

What the evidence does and does not support is important. It supports a consistent association between being married or cohabiting and higher fertility desire/intention in several studies and meta-analyses [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-F3]. It does not support a universal, fixed effect across all HIV-positive populations; instead, it supports a general pattern that is sensitive to region, age, treatment status, and other covariates [N1-F1][N3-F3]. It also does not support a simple “married people always have higher fertility intentions” conclusion; rather, it supports a nuanced interpretation that married individuals are more likely to have higher fertility intentions than unmarried peers, but the strength and direction may differ by context [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence on unmarried HIV-positive fertility intention shows that unmarried individuals generally have lower or more constrained fertility intentions than married peers, and that unmarried status is often treated as a broader category.

The most direct evidence comes from the 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis, which reports that marital status was associated with fertility desire and that PLHIV who are married or cohabiting had higher fertility desire than single, widowed, or divorced individuals [N3-F3]. It also reports that the pooled odds ratio for marital status was 1.34 (95% CI: 1.08–1.66) [N3-F3]. This indicates that unmarried individuals are less likely to have higher fertility desire than married individuals. Another study excerpt similarly states that PLHIV who are married or cohabiting have more fertility desire than HIV-infected people who are single, widowed, or divorced [N6-F3]. This suggests that unmarried status is associated with lower fertility intention in the literature.

On levels of fertility intention, the evidence is not explicit about exact percentages for unmarried individuals, but it does show that married/cohabiting people are more likely to desire fertility. The 2021 meta-analysis also reports that fertility desire was associated with being childless, younger age, being on ART, being male, and having fewer children [N3-F3]. This implies that unmarried individuals may be part of a group with higher childlessness and lower fertility desire, but the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of mean intention scores across marital statuses. The evidence also suggests that unmarried individuals may be more likely to delay or avoid pregnancy, especially because fertility desire is tied to reproductive decision-making and preventive care [N3-F3].

How unmarried status is defined matters. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis explicitly combines single, divorced, and widowed individuals into one analytic group because these individuals were not married and had similar HIV-related characteristics [N3-R5]. This definition is important because it means the comparison is not only between married and single people, but also between married and a broader unmarried category that includes divorced and widowed individuals. The evidence therefore supports a comparison between married people and a composite “not married” group, rather than a precise single/divorced/widowed comparison in every study [N3-R5].

In summary, the evidence indicates that unmarried HIV-positive individuals tend to have lower fertility desire than married individuals, and unmarried status is usually treated as a combined category of single, divorced, and widowed people [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The evidence also suggests that unmarried individuals may be more likely to delay or avoid pregnancy, but it does not provide detailed data on intention levels for each subgroup [N3-F3].

Marriage appears to influence fertility intentions through social support, decision-making, and contraceptive use, while HIV-related stigma and disclosure may vary by marital status, and reproductive health services and family planning access may differ accordingly.

First, marriage is associated with social support and decision-making. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis emphasizes that marital status is a prominent factor shaping fertility intentions [N1-F1]. The 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis likewise notes that marital status was strongly associated with fertility desire and reports that married/cohabiting PLHIV had higher fertility desire than single, widowed, or divorced individuals [N3-F3]. This suggests that marriage may provide a social context in which individuals feel more supported to pursue fertility, have greater partner involvement, or experience less pressure to avoid reproduction. The evidence also highlights that reproductive decision-making is influenced by family planning needs and autonomy [N5-R4], and that open communication about family planning is necessary [N5-R4]. Marriage may therefore create a more structured environment for reproductive planning.

Second, HIV-related stigma and disclosure may vary by marital status. The evidence indicates that HIV-related stigma and disclosure can affect fertility desire [N2-R3]. A study excerpt specifically mentions that fertility desire mediated the association between HIV-related stigma and fertility intention among couples living with HIV [N2-R3]. This implies that married individuals may face different stigma dynamics than unmarried individuals, perhaps because disclosure to a partner can reduce perceived stigma and increase willingness to plan fertility. The evidence also suggests that disclosure to sexual partners can affect fertility desire [N3-F3], reinforcing the idea that marital status shapes how individuals experience HIV-related stigma and disclosure.

Third, reproductive health services and family planning access may differ by marital status. The evidence on family planning and HIV integration shows that integrating family planning into HIV services can increase access to contraception among clients of HIV services [N5-R5]. Prepregnancy counseling and care for people with HIV include considerations for contraceptives, ART, and infant feeding [N5-R1], and preconception counseling emphasizes reducing HIV transmission risk while conceiving [N5-R3]. These services are likely more accessible to married individuals because marriage often correlates with greater engagement in reproductive health systems, more stable partnerships, and greater likelihood of receiving partner-based counseling [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence also emphasizes that access to reproductive health services and autonomous decision-making are important for family planning [N5-R4]. Thus, married individuals may have better access to services that support fertility intentions, while unmarried individuals may face barriers such as less access to integrated services, less partner support, or less stable contraceptive counseling.

In conclusion, married people may have higher fertility intentions because marriage provides social support and decision-making context, because HIV-related stigma and disclosure may differ by marital status, and because reproductive health services and family planning access may be more favorable for married individuals [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## Integrated final answer

The evidence supports the finding that married people living with HIV generally have higher fertility intentions compared to those with other marital statuses, but the support is best understood as general and context-sensitive rather than universal. Across multiple studies and meta-analyses, married or cohabiting people living with HIV are consistently associated with higher fertility desire or intention than single, widowed, or divorced peers [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-F3]. This pattern is not simply a statistical artifact; it reflects a recurring association in the literature that has been reinforced by systematic reviews and pooled analyses of PLHIV fertility intentions [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### 1) Direct evidence that married HIV-positive people have higher fertility intentions

The strongest direct evidence comes from two major reviews and meta-analyses. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 25 articles with 11,394 participants found that marital status was associated with higher fertility intention, with an odds ratio of 1.52 (95% CI: 1.14–2.02) [N1-F1]. A separate 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 50 articles with 22,367 subjects also reported that marital status was associated with fertility desire, with an odds ratio of 1.34 (95% CI: 1.08–1.66) [N3-F3]. Another study excerpt explicitly states that married or cohabiting PLHIV had more fertility desire than HIV-infected people who were single, widowed, or divorced [N6-F3]. Together, these sources show a consistent direction of association: married status is linked to higher fertility intentions.

The evidence is strongest when marital status is treated as a categorical indicator of fertility desire or intention. However, the measurement is not always identical across studies. The 2024 review uses pooled odds ratios for fertility intention, but the evidence excerpt does not specify the exact measurement instrument used in each study [N1-F1]. The 2021 meta-analysis similarly reports pooled odds ratios and random-effects models, with subgroup analyses and sensitivity assessments, but it does not detail every study’s measurement tool [N3-F3]. This means the evidence is reasonably consistent in direction, but not always fully comparable in detail.

### 2) Why married people may have higher fertility intentions

The branch evidence explains this pattern through social support, decision-making, stigma/disclosure, and access to reproductive health services.

#### Social support and decision-making
Marriage is associated with a more structured reproductive context. The 2024 review notes that marital status is a prominent factor shaping fertility intentions [N1-F1], and the 2021 meta-analysis reports that married/cohabiting PLHIV had higher fertility desire than single, widowed, or divorced individuals [N3-F3]. This suggests that marriage may provide social support, partner involvement, and a framework for reproductive decision-making. The family planning literature also emphasizes that open communication about family planning needs and desires is necessary, and that access to reproductive health services and autonomous decision-making are important for family planning [N5-R4].

#### HIV-related stigma and disclosure
HIV-related stigma and disclosure may vary by marital status, which can influence fertility intentions. A study excerpt explicitly states that fertility desire mediated the association between HIV-related stigma and fertility intention among couples living with HIV [N2-R3]. This implies that married individuals may experience different stigma dynamics than unmarried individuals, potentially because disclosure to a partner can reduce perceived stigma and increase willingness to plan fertility. The evidence also notes that disclosure to sexual partners can affect fertility desire [N3-F3], reinforcing the idea that marital status shapes how people experience HIV-related stigma.

#### Reproductive health services and family planning access
Reproductive health services and family planning access are likely more favorable for married individuals. The evidence on HIV-related reproductive health services shows that integrating family planning into HIV services can increase access to contraception among clients of HIV services [N5-R5]. Prepregnancy counseling and care for people with HIV includes considerations for contraceptives, ART, and infant feeding [N5-R1], and preconception counseling emphasizes reducing HIV transmission risk while conceiving [N5-R3]. These services are likely more accessible to married individuals because marriage often correlates with greater engagement in reproductive health systems, more stable partnerships, and greater likelihood of receiving partner-based counseling [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence also emphasizes that access to reproductive health services and autonomous decision-making are important for family planning [N5-R4].

### 3) How unmarried HIV-positive individuals compare

The evidence on unmarried HIV-positive fertility intention shows that unmarried individuals generally have lower or more constrained fertility intentions than married peers. The 2021 meta-analysis reports that married/cohabiting PLHIV had higher fertility desire than single, widowed, or divorced individuals [N3-F3], and it explicitly combines single, divorced, and widowed individuals into one analytic group because these individuals were not married and had similar HIV-related characteristics [N3-R5]. This definition is important: it means the comparison is not only between married and single people, but also between married and a broader unmarried category that includes divorced and widowed individuals [N3-R5].

On levels of fertility intention, the evidence is not explicit about exact percentages for unmarried individuals, but it does show that married/cohabiting people are more likely to desire fertility. The 2021 meta-analysis also reports that fertility desire was associated with being childless, younger age, being on ART, being male, and having fewer children [N3-F3]. This implies that unmarried individuals may be part of a group with higher childlessness and lower fertility desire, but the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of mean intention scores across marital statuses [N3-F3]. It does, however, suggest that unmarried individuals may be more likely to delay or avoid pregnancy, especially because fertility desire is tied to reproductive decision-making and preventive care [N3-F3].

### 4) Limitations and what the evidence does not support

The evidence base is useful but has important limitations. First, most of the evidence is observational and cross-sectional, so it cannot establish causality [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Second, study design varies: the 2024 review included 25 articles with 11,394 participants, while the 2021 review included 50 articles with 22,367 subjects, but both note heterogeneity and variability in educational classifications across countries [N1-F1][N3-F3].
